questions.q: Why does the STAR format apply beyond just the capstone technical story?
options: It doesn't - STAR only works for the capstone
STAR is only used for written answers, never spoken ones
STAR only applies to questions about software features
STAR is a general-purpose structure (Situation, Task, Action, Result) that works for any behavioral question requiring a real example
questions.explain: STAR is a general structure for telling any work story - it applies to behavioral questions about pressure, mistakes, ambiguity, and communication just as well as to the capstone.

questions.q: For 'tell me about a time you had to deliver difficult news,' what approach does this lesson recommend?
options: Avoid mentioning anything negative ever happened
Blame another team entirely for the bad news
Name the hard truth plainly and pair it with a credible plan, following through visibly
Promise an unrealistic timeline just to sound reassuring
questions.explain: The recommended approach is directness paired with a credible plan - naming what's wrong plainly rather than softening or hiding it, then following through.

questions.q: What distinguishes a strong answer to 'describe a time requirements were ambiguous' from a weak one?
options: A strong answer complains at length about how confusing the requirements were
A weak answer lists every stakeholder's name in detail
A strong answer describes specifically how you narrowed the ambiguity - clarifying questions, documenting what was agreed, flagging scope changes early
There is no meaningful difference between the two
questions.explain: A strong answer focuses on the concrete steps taken to narrow ambiguity, not just on describing how confusing or frustrating the situation was.

questions.q: When answering 'tell me about a time you made a mistake,' where should most of the answer's weight go?
options: Entirely on detailed excuses for why the mistake wasn't really your fault
On minimizing the mistake so it sounds unimportant
On naming every other person who was also partially responsible
On what you changed afterward, after plainly owning the mistake in one sentence
questions.explain: A believable answer owns the mistake plainly and briefly, then spends the majority of the answer on what specifically changed as a result.

questions.q: Why is the capstone's January 31 crisis useful material for a behavioral question like 'tell me about a time you worked under pressure,' not just technical questions?
options: Because it involved a tight deadline, multiple real interconnected problems, and the need to communicate findings clearly to a stakeholder under pressure
Because behavioral questions are never actually asked in real interviews
Because the capstone has no connection to any stakeholder communication
Because technical stories and behavioral stories must always use completely different examples
questions.explain: The capstone's pressure, complexity, and stakeholder communication make it strong material for behavioral 'under pressure' questions, not just technical ones.
